{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Tokushima Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōasahiko Shrine
大麻比古神社 | image = Ohoasahikojinja.jpg | caption = Ōasahiko Shrine's ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Tokushima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|10|15.50|N|134|30|9.25|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Ōasahiko-no-Okami
[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} [[file:Ōasahiko-jinja torii.jpeg|thumb|right|Ōasahiko Shrine's main ''[[torii]]'']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Tokushima Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōasahiko Shrine
大麻比古神社 | image = Ohoasahikojinja.jpg | caption = Ōasahiko Shrine's ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Tokushima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|10|15.50|N|134|30|9.25|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Ōasahiko-no-Okami
[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} [[file:Ōasahiko-jinja torii.jpeg|thumb|right|Ōasahiko Shrine's main ''[[torii]]'']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commonscat|Ōasahiko-jinja|Ōasahiko Shrine}} *[http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/ Official home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] ]] ]] {{Inbe Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Awa Province (Tokushima)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:bgoodbye $1]] [[Category:Naruto, Tokushima]] [[Category:Inbe clan]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[Category:1 revision imported]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[en:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[ja:Ōasahiko Shrine]]

The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. 大麻比古神社 | image = Ohoasahikojinja.jpg | caption = Ōasahiko Shrine's ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Tokushima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|10|15.50|N|134|30|9.25|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Ōasahiko-no-Okami
[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} [[file:Ōasahiko-jinja torii.jpeg|thumb|right|Ōasahiko Shrine's main ''[[torii]]'']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commonscat|Ōasahiko-jinja|Ōasahiko Shrine}} *[http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/ Official home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] ]] ]] {{Inbe Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Awa Province (Tokushima)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:bgoodbye $1]] [[Category:Naruto, Tokushima]] [[Category:Inbe clan]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]][[Category:qq]] }} [[en:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[ja:Ōasahiko Shrine]]

Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. [[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} [[file:Ōasahiko-jinja torii.jpeg|thumb|right|Ōasahiko Shrine's main ''[[torii]]'']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official Ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official Ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commonscat|Ōasahiko-jinja|Ōasahiko Shrine}} *[http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/ Official home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] ]] ]] {{Inbe Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Awa Province (Tokushima)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Naruto, Tokushima]] [[Category:Inbe clan]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[en:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[ja:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[sn: failed]]

{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Tokushima Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōasahiko Shrine
大麻比古神社 | image = Ohoasahikojinja.jpg | caption = Ōasahiko Shrine's ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Tokushima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|10|15.50|N|134|30|9.25|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Ōasahiko-no-Okami
[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} [[file:Ōasahiko-jinja torii.jpeg|thumb|right|Ōasahiko Shrine's main ''[[torii]]'']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official Ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commonscat|Ōasahiko-jinja|Ōasahiko Shrine}} *[http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/ Official home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] ]] ]] {{Inbe Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Awa Province (Tokushima)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Naruto, Tokushima]] [[Category:Inbe clan]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]][[Category:qq]] }} [[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[en:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[ja:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[sn: failed]]

{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Tokushima Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōasahiko Shrine
大麻比古神社 | image = Ohoasahikojinja.jpg | caption = Ōasahiko Shrine's ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Tokushima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|10|15.50|N|134|30|9.25|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Ōasahiko-no-Okami
[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} [[file:Ōasahiko-jinja torii.jpeg|thumb|right|Ōasahiko Shrine's main ''[[torii]]'']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official Ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commonscat|Ōasahiko-jinja|Ōasahiko Shrine}} *[http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/ Official home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] ]] ]] {{Inbe Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Awa Province (Tokushima)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Naruto, Tokushima]] [[Category:Inbe clan]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]][[Category:qq]] }} [[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[en:Ōasahiko Shrine]] [[sn:asahiko Shrine]] [[sn: failed]] [[Category:Ja import failed]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Ōasahiko Shrine]][[Category:qq]]

After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. [[Sarutahiko Ōkami|Sarutahiko-no-Okami]] | founded_by = | established = late [[Heian period]] | date_destroyed = | location =13 Aza Hirotsuka, Bando Oasa-cho, Naruto-shi Tokushima-ken 779-0230 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = November 1 | leadership = }} '']] {{Nihongo|'''Ōasahiko Shrine'''|大麻比古神社|Ōasahiko-jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Ōasachō-Bandō neighborhood of the city of [[Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on November 1.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} {{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Ōasahiko Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''Ōasahiko-no-Okami'''| 大宜都比売命|}}, the goddess of food * {{nihongo|[[Sarutahiko Ōkami|'''Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami''']]|猿田彦大神|}} It is believed that in the era of [[Emperor Jimmu]], [[Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto]] came to the [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa region]] (an ancient region that encompassed most of present-day [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) seeking fertilized land to sow hemp seeds. The planted seeds were then cultivated by the area's population so they could produce linen called [[Apocynum cannabinum|''asa'']], which formed the base of the area's industry. Because of the impact he had on furthering the welfare of Japan, Ōasahiko Shrine was dedicated in the area to worship him as a ''[[kami]]'' named Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami. The secondary ''kami'' enshrined at Ōasahiko is [[Sarutahiko|Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami]]. He is depicted as standing at the junction of heaven and earth to guide the grandchildren of [[Amaterasu]], the Imperial Family and the founders of the human race to earth. He is primarily known for greeting and guiding [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]], grandson of Amaterasu, to earth.{{cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/~gwilliams/tsa/Kami_no_Michi_8.html |title=Sarutahiko Ōkami |accessdate=2008-08-21 |author=Yamamoto, Yukitaka}} After his various achievements, he was enshrined at Ōasahiko Shrine along with Ōasahiko-no-Okami.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/e/yuisho/ |title=Original history |accessdate=2008-08-21}} ==History== The exact year of the foundation of Ōasahiko Shrine is unknown. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' national history which was compiled in 901, in entries dated 867, 878, and 883, noting promotions in its official ranking. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', written in 927, it is listed as a {{nihongo|'''[[Myojin Taisha]]'''|名神大社||}}. During the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Kamakura period]], it was designated the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. Under the premodern system of ''[[shinbutsu-shūgō]]'' syncretism between Buddhism and Shinto, it was closely associated with [[Ryōzen-ji (Naruto)|Ryōzen-ji]], the first temple in the [[Shikoku pilgrimage]] and ''[[jingū-ji]]'' to the shrine. It was supported in the [[Muromachi period|Muromachi]], [[Sengoku period|Sengoku]] and [[Edo period]] by the [[Hosokawa clan]], [[Miyoshi clan]] and [[Hachisuka clan]], continued to improve its shrine rating until it was awarded the 1st grade in 1719. Following the [[Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} in 1871 under [[State Shinto]]'s [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] .{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} This qualified it for government support, and it was able to reconstruct most of its buildings in 1890. After the abolition State Shinto after World War II, the shrine became a [[Beppyo shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], and in 1970, the current ''[[Honden]]'', ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'' and the ''Gaihaiden'' were rebuilt from the donations of worshipers. Since then, Ōasahiko Shrine has lost most of its national importance, but remains today as an important place of worship in the Tokushima area. The shrine is 25-minute walk from [[Bandō Station]] on the [[JR Shikoku]] [[Kōtoku Line]]. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Features== [[file:Doitsu-bashi.jpeg|thumb|right|German Bridge]] Marking the start of an 800-meter-long (2,625 ft) road leading directly to the shrine's ''haiden'' is a large, orange ''[[torii]]''. By using [[reinforced concrete]] and [[steel]], this ''torii'' was first constructed in 1958 and had a height of {{convert|15.6|m|ft|0}} and a width of {{convert|11|m|ft|0}}. Because of its deteriorated state, it was reconstructed in 2002 using metal tubing. The access road which follows is lined with dozens of stone [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]] donated by shrine parishioners in 2004-05.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/qa/ |title=Q&A |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} In the center of the shrine grounds is a 1000-year-old [[camphor tree]] known as {{Nihongo|''Go-[[shinboku]]''|ご神木}}. This revered tree's main trunk has a circumference of {{convert|8.3|m|ft|0}} and a maximum height of {{convert|22|m|ft|0}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.ooasahikojinja.jp/map/# |script-title=ja:境内案内図 |accessdate=2008-08-21 |language=Japanese}} Behind the main portion of the shrine grounds to the northeast is the {{Nihongo|''German Bridge''|ドイツ橋|Doitsu bashi}}. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]]. This stone bridge was built by the [[POW]]s who were held captive at the camp. ==Gallery== Oasahiko-jinja, honden-2.jpg|Honden Oasahiko-jinja, kusu.jpg|Great camphor tree (Naruto city Natural Monument) Oasahiko-jinja, haiden-3.jpg| Gaihaiden Oasahiko-jinja, torii.jpg|Inner torii Haraigawabashi Bridge in front of Oasahiko Shrine.JPG|Haraigawabashi Bridge ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. From April 1917 to December 1919, about 953 German and Austro-Hungarian soldiers were imprisoned at the nearby [[Bandō Prisoner of War camp]] during [[World War I]].
